subjects.introduction: Even the poorest giver and the smallest gift, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, should bring the giver joy. That moves the question of generosity away from the size of a purse toward the condition of a heart. The believer is to shine like the sun on every land without condition, to share a word or a gem that others lack as readily as bread, to be a flowing spring to the thirsty and a comfort to the wayfarer, kind to stranger and kin alike. Justice gives every rightful claimant his due; munificence, which Bahá’u’lláh ranks above it, adds what love freely bestows. A gift can also wound, and the Qur’án warns against following charity with reproach, so that the manner of giving becomes part of its meaning [1]. Whoever has something shares it, and whoever has nothing gives thanks; and giving, strangely, turns out to be the cause of receiving. From here the journey leads into compassion and kindness, into voluntary giving and the charitable associations that organise it, and into the selfishness that generosity quietly undoes.
subjects.arc: Start with the joy of a small gift, widen the circle of giving, and explore generosity as justice fulfilled and love freely offered.

order.why: Widen the gift through the sun’s image of unconditional bounty.
shortened: Like the sun, he must shine on all and bestow his light on every land. You see that the infinite mercy of God embraces the whole of creation and knows no bias. The people of Baha must be the manifestations of this mercy and perform their charity similarly without any condition or intent.

order.why: Begin with the accessible joy of giving, however small one’s means.
shortened: Giving should be a joy to the giver, however poor he maybe, or however small his gift.

order.why: Let a word as well as a material treasure become something to share.
shortened: If you possess a word or gem that others are deprived of, share it with them in utmost kindliness and goodwill.

order.why: Give universal generosity the concrete forms of relief and welcome.
shortened: She spent her wealth upon the weak and the poor, seeking Thy good pleasure.
Her generosity was as a flowing spring to every thirsty soul, and a comfort to every wanderer and wayfarer.

order.why: Connect gratitude with care for strangers, relatives, and the poor.
Extend the reach of charity beyond a preferred circle.
shortened: Grace, generosity, favor and charity should be universal - surely this is more pleasing and attractive.

order.why: Pause over the distinction between another person’s due and a freely bestowed gift.
Uses the generous earth as an image for trustworthy, forbearing character and calls on the recipient to embody it.
Complicate easy judgments about generosity by considering opportunity and resources.
Hold the invitation to give beside gratitude in times of lack.
shortened: If thou findest a bounty from the grace of thy Lord, give freely thereof; and if thou findest not, then be thankful.

order.why: Urges honesty and sharing divine bounty with the poor rather than depriving them.
Preserve the separate source’s closely related counsel as a deliberate echo.
shortened: The mystic asked: "How then do you and your friends fare?" He replied: "When we find something we share it, and when we lack we give thanks."

order.why: Consider the relationship between giving and blessing.
Present generosity as an education of the person who gives.
Distinguish universal material generosity from the passage’s devotional account of sacrifice.
Place self-sacrifice within the generous bestowal of perfections upon all peoples.
End the linked readings with a paradox whose full context concerns receiving spiritual food.
Resume with the memorable image of hands adorned by generosity.
Reconsider the grounds on which a person deserves esteem.
shortened: O ye who are near to the Divine Threshold! Your letter was received, and the enclosed note caused great joy, that this esteemed person made such an undertaking and made such a contribution.

Likewise observe how the power of God's Cause is becoming evident and manifest, that such an illustrious person would make such a sacrifice for a place where that perfumed body was entrusted for one or two nights - this purified body that for fifty years, out of fear of the enemies' desecration, could not be placed anywhere, for the enemies were lying in wait and had they gotten hold of it they would have burned it.

questions: How do the opening passages change what we count as a gift, and who we imagine is able to give?
What is the relationship between meeting another person’s rightful claim and offering something beyond it?
How might a giver protect another person’s freedom and dignity, especially when resources or power are unequal?
What could the images of spiritual food and a growing tree teach us about receiving, giving, and the lasting effects of a small deed?

neighbors.invitation: Follow generosity into the welcome that gives a simple meal its value.
Examine the wish to serve without seeking recognition.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 2:262 — giving without reproach
references.note: This verse joins giving for God’s sake with care not to injure or reproach the recipient. Read it beside the sun’s unconditional bounty and the distinction between justice and munificence: how does the manner of a gift become part of its meaning? Several English translations are provided.

subjects.introduction: If every meal were the same dish, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá remarks, food would grow tedious; diversity, rightly understood, is harmony itself. One person looks at stones and sees only clay, while another sees the hand of the Creator, and the same tree speaks of the sun to one and of rain to another. Religions differ, He explains, because minds differ, and a single encompassing power of understanding could bring their judgements together. Invited to America for the sake of its flowers, He replied that a good gardener first arranges the garden before welcoming a guest, and asked for prayers that harmony might grow among those varied blooms. John Stuart Mill argued that opinions we oppose may hold a part of the truth we lack [1]. Between these lies a demanding art. It opens into consultation, where differing views are meant to meet, into the limits of criticism, and into that unity in diversity which is the mark of a living whole.
subjects.arc: Enter through the pleasure of variety, encounter different perspectives, and ask how thoughtful fellowship can become harmony.

order.why: Distinguishes unity from forced uniformity and explains the limits of outward pressure.
Make the value of variety immediately tangible through the image of food.
A direct explanation of how differences in ideas and opinions enrich a unified community.
Show how different observers understand the same material world.
shortened: You see a man whose interest and view is centered around stone and clay; still another man who looks at stones, he thinks about the Creator, how expert to create such wonders. Another who looks at trees. He thinks of the effect and energy of the sun the effect of the breeze that blows; the influence and effect of rain' who has educated these trees. Viewpoints are different.

order.why: Explains differences of understanding through the capacities of recipients, using the river and mirror analogies.
Explicitly accepts differing understandings of revelation while rejecting quarrels over them.
Urges nurturing and accepting people whose understanding differs, even when they do not advance to another’s position.
Distinguishes freedom of thought from conduct, retaining the stated limits of courtesy and law.
A concise rejection of coerced religious belief.
Explicitly rejects fighting over differences of thought, belief or custom.
Directly addresses freedom to express differing opinions and their value in reaching a decision.
A practical account of consultation, receptiveness to better views and the fallibility of majority opinion.
Explains respectful disagreement within an assembly and preserves the accompanying rule about implementing its decisions.
A concrete response about continuing association across religious boundaries.
Proposes reciprocal visits to houses of worship as a practical remedy for religious misunderstanding.
The complete Abraham and aged guest story illustrates patience toward a different belief.
Bring diversity into a concrete historical account of affectionate fellowship.
The sun and its changing dawning points illustrate openness to truth beyond a familiar religious form.
The many entrances to one temple offer a distinct illustration of diverse religious approaches.
The physician analogy explains why differing religious laws need not imply conflicting purposes.
Ask what kind of understanding could encompass competing religious opinions.
End with the task of arranging a varied garden into a harmonious whole.
shortened: Thou hast invited me to America saying that in that region and in that country there are many fragrant and multicolored flowers, likewise there are thorns and thistles but Abdul-Baha should not look upon the thistles of the desert. But He should hasten to that county for the sake of the flowers. This simile is very beautiful but when a gardener invites a man to his garden first he will arrange all the flowers with the utmost elegance, beauty and art, then he will invite his guest. Moreover, there are differences among the flowers, therefore, pray thou that harmony may be created among the flowers so that that country may find capacity for the presence of Abdul-Baha.

questions: What do the food and garden images reveal about diversity, and where might those images leave the difficulty of real disagreement unresolved?
How could a group welcome different convictions while continuing to examine their truth and consequences?
How might attention to language, context, and the limits of one’s perspective change a conversation with someone whose beliefs differ sharply from one’s own?

neighbors.invitation: Consider how attachment to words can conceal the meanings another person is trying to convey.
Explore the work of reading an apparent tension within a larger whole.

references.label: 1 · John Stuart Mill, On Liberty, chapter II
references.note: Near the end of chapter II, Mill considers the partial truth an opposing opinion may contain and the way unchallenged beliefs become lifeless. Compare his defense of open disagreement with the compilation’s aspiration to harmony. What practices would allow each concern to illuminate the other?

subjects.introduction: Bodies found in the pyramids, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá observed, show the same characteristics as people living today; the span of human life does not change from age to age, and the vast ages given to biblical figures must be read as religious cycles rather than as a report on flesh. That steadiness of the human frame across millennia is the setting for a far larger claim: the human form is the greatest proof of God in creation, a Book written by His own hand, a Temple reared by His wisdom, a compendium of every world and an epitome of the Well-Guarded Tablet. To live in such a body is to carry sacred meaning about in the ordinary business of eating, working and resting. Other passages examine bodily composition and the organs as instruments of the soul, tracing illness, aging, death, and the interdependence of different faculties. Paul’s image of the body as a temple of the Holy Spirit, with its consequences for conduct, sits naturally beside this and lets the two traditions be compared without being collapsed into one [1]. What such reverence asks of us, in the care we give ourselves and other creatures, leads on to the human being as microcosm of the greater world, as the sum and fruit of creation, and to the long story of human evolution.
subjects.arc: Move from bodily composition and development through the faculties and the soul to interdependence, sacred imagery, and respect for the body.

order.why: Contrasts bodily frailty with spiritual capacity.
Begin with the historical conversation and its context for reading biblical ages.
Describes bodily composition and the relation of animal and human faculties.
Discusses physical evolution alongside spiritual development.
Describes bodily composition and decomposition in the cycle of life and death.
Distinguishes the names soul, mind, and spirit by their functions.
Directly explains the organs as instruments through which the spirit operates.
Distinguishes the condition of bodily faculties from the independence of the soul.
Explains why changing bodily powers and health do not change the spirit itself.
Addresses the effect of old age on the organs through which the spirit functions.
Contrasts the spatial body with the soul that is not confined to place.
Explains death as the severing of the connection between body and soul.
Connects rational perception with the outward and inward senses.
Explains the changing names of a single faculty in relation to different organs.
Uses the interdependence of bodily organs to explain mutual effects in the universe.
Explains how the diversity of bodily organs contributes to unity and beauty.
Uses simultaneous bodily faculties to illustrate the manifestation of divine names.
Presents the human body as an index of the greater world.
Interprets the human frame as containing the signs of the wider universe.
Explains why the body deserves respect after death.
Let the final reading enlarge the physical form through its layered sacred images.

questions: What changes in our care for ourselves and other living beings when we read the body as both a physical reality and a bearer of sacred meaning?
How do the passages distinguish changes in bodily organs from the capacities attributed to the soul?
What can bodily interdependence teach us about unity, and where should that analogy be used with care?

neighbors.invitation: Consider how bodily and spiritual life belong within a search for balance.
Extend reflection on embodied life to the feelings and needs of animals.

references.label: 1 · 1 Corinthians 6:19–20 — the body as temple
references.note: Paul connects the temple image with the Holy Spirit, belonging to God, and bodily conduct. Compare the responsibilities suggested by that image with the second reading’s book, temple, and bridge; consider what each metaphor adds without assuming identical accounts of the human person.

subjects.displayTitle: Pure intentions in teaching the Cause
subjects.introduction: What is left of the wish to serve when no one is watching? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá answers by asking for service to every human being from the depth of the soul, not because people will recognise a good deed but because the Blessed Beauty has wished it. Everything else about teaching rests on that inward direction. The teacher’s intention must be pure, his heart independent, his thought at peace, his resolve firm; given that, a sanctified breath will affect even a rock, and without it there will be no result at all. The claim is startling, and it is meant to turn attention from technique to character. A soul concentrated on God becomes a fountain of living water for a thirsty world, and intentions working for the good of all, cut loose from the earth, become light and delicate as spirit. Jesus asked that alms be given so quietly that the left hand does not know what the right is doing [1], the same examination of audience. Purity of motive is never finished; it is purged daily, and it opens onto purity of heart, sincerity of intention, and the detachment that lets a teacher serve before feeling perfected.
subjects.arc: Begin with service that seeks no recognition, examine the teacher’s inward life, and return to the daily cultivation of sincere motives.

order.why: Explore the inward qualities and consistency demanded of a teacher.
shortened: The aim is this: The intention of the teacher must be pure, his heart independent, his spirit attracted, his thought at peace, his resolution firm, his magnanimity exalted and in the love of God a shining torch. Should he become as such, his sanctified breath will even affect the rock; otherwise there will be no result whatsoever. As long as a soul is not perfected, how can he efface the defects of others? Unless he is detached from aught else save God, how can he teach severance to others?

order.why: Open with the direct test of service without recognition.
Give intention a universal aim in the good of all.
Places pure intention alongside love, truthfulness and sincerity in teaching across peoples and communities.
Makes freedom from financial reward or recompense a concrete condition of the teacher's detachment.
Retain the distinct account of the teacher’s qualities as a concise echo.
shortened: The intention of the teacher must be pure, his heart independent, his spirit attracted, his thoughts at peace, his resolution firm, his magnanimity exalted, and in the love of God a shining torch.

order.why: A concise statement that sanctity, purity and visible sincerity are what allow the teacher to influence hearts.
Connects freedom from self-interest with understanding the listener's literature, customs and standpoint.
Let the fountain image connect inner concentration with a world’s need.
shortened: Concentrate the soul upon God so that it may become as a fountain pouring out the Water of Life to a thirsty world.

order.why: Bring the account of spiritual influence to its most arresting image.
shortened: A pure soul will affect even stone and the ray of the Sun of Truth will pierce mountains.

order.why: End with daily effort as the means of cultivating love, truthfulness, and purity of motive.

questions: How might we recognize the difference between serving another person and seeking confirmation of our own importance?
What do peace of mind, firmness of resolve, and concern for the good of all contribute to a conversation about belief?
How could daily self-examination help us grow in sincerity while remaining willing to serve before we feel perfected?

neighbors.invitation: Consider how inner sincerity becomes warmth, patience, and friendship.
Give the examination of motives a daily practice of review and renewal.

references.label: 1 · Matthew 6:1–4 — the audience for a good deed
references.note: The Sermon on the Mount examines charity performed to win public praise. Read it beside service for God’s good pleasure in the opening selection. How can a visible example benefit others while the wish for admiration remains under examination?

subjects.introduction: Sunlight falling on a flat mirror warms nothing, but gathered by a lens to a single point it burns. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá uses that image for the mind: scattered thoughts achieve no result, and attention concentrated on one thing becomes a force. The same holds for water gathered into a single fountain, for the student of an art who cannot learn it while half attending to something else, and for anyone who wishes truly to serve God. Yet the capacity to focus raises a second question, what deserves it, and here the answer is remembrance: the first thought on waking, the presence of the Almighty known before a prayer begins rather than the birds outside the window, a heart that is not heedless of God for a single moment, in standing and sitting, sleeping and waking. Such attention does not retreat from work; the ploughman’s hands and feet are busy in the field while his heart stays with the Beloved. The Bhagavad Gita’s counsel to bring the wandering mind back, again and again, to the Self describes a kindred discipline with its own account of the goal [1]. Mindfulness also means noticing consequences and learning from yesterday, so that heedlessness does not injure a shared life. The path continues into contemplation and meditation, into composure and serenity, and into the discipline of self-perfection.
subjects.arc: Gather the mind’s scattered energies, give attention a devotional purpose, and carry it into work and responsibility for others.

order.why: Open with focused sunlight as an immediate image of attention’s power. Return to the opening image, now informed by devotion, work, and care.
shortened: So long as the thoughts of an individual are scattered he will achieve no results, but if his thinking be concentrated on a single point wonderful will be the fruits thereof.

One cannot obtain the full force of the sunlight when it is cast on a flat mirror, but once the sun shineth upon a concave mirror, or on a lens that is convex, all its heat will be concentrated on a single point, and that one point will burn the hottest. Thus is it necessary to focus one's thinking on a single point so that it will become an effective force.

order.why: Recast gathered strength through water concentrated in a fountain.
shortened: Focus your thoughts on this matter, for this is what is beneficial now. Do not scatter your thoughts. If you scatter your thoughts you will not succeed in any one thing. When water is concentrated in one fountain, the fountain becomes very powerful and gushes forth strongly, but when divided among multiple fountains, none of the fountains gains strength.

order.why: Connect concentration with learning an art and dedicating oneself to service.
shortened: When man wishes to accomplish something, he must give himself entirely to that thing. For instance, if one desires to learn art, he must concentrate all his faculties and mind upon it; he cannot do that and something else at the same time. So when a man wishes truly to serve God, he must concentrate all his mind upon this service and think of nothing else whatever.

order.why: Move from the capacity to concentrate to the direction of a day’s first thought.
Gives a concrete discipline of opposing thoughts of war and hatred with stronger thoughts of peace and love.
Examine the competing distractions present in prayer.
Give inward attention the language of remembrance in the heart.
Consider the intensity of an unbroken spiritual discipline.
shortened: And the greatest spiritual discipline in this regard is that thy heart not be heedless of God's remembrance for a single moment.

order.why: Extend recollection to the intimate rhythm of breathing.
shortened: Take no rest except in remembrance of God. This is what the Dove of the Spirit counseleth you that haply ye may be guided by the guidance of God, and may conduct yourselves upon the earth in accordance with His will. This is better for you than all that hath been and will be. And take no breath except in remembrance of the Beloved, if ye would be guided by this counsel.

order.why: Follow remembrance through waking, sleeping, standing, and sitting.
shortened: O My handmaiden! Remember thy Lord in thy standing and thy sitting, in thy sleep and thy wakefulness.

order.why: Sustain the invitation to remembrance across time.
shortened: God willing, thou shalt be mentioned among the people through the name of Truth and be accounted among the servants of the divine Cause, in such wise that at all times thou shalt be occupied with the remembrance of the All-Merciful.

order.why: Enter the field where work and inward devotion meet.
shortened: When you are plowing the ground or sowing the seeds or reaping the harvest let all your thoughts and subconscious thinking be of God.

order.why: Keep the separate account and its explicit relationship between working limbs and an attached heart.
Turn sustained thought toward an opportunity to serve.
shortened: Think day and night how thou mayest render some service at the Sacred Threshold.

order.why: Widen mindfulness to every condition of life.
shortened: Man must be mindful in all conditions.

order.why: Connects concentrated attention in prayer with awareness of conversing with God.
Join attention with humility about consequences and learning from the past.
shortened: Since one has no encompassing knowledge of the consequences of affairs, therefore one must always take the path of mindfulness and wisdom, and learn lessons from the past for the future.

order.why: Confront the social cost of thoughtlessness.
Answer that cost with a prayer for awakening.
shortened: O God! Awaken us from the deep slumber of negligence! Suffer us to become mindful and aware!

order.why: Close the linked readings with remembrance that awakens others.
Allow the supplied image of prayer in the wilderness to open space for recollection.

questions: What distinguishes the ability to concentrate from wisdom about where to place our attention?
How might the passages about plowing and harvesting change our understanding of remembrance during ordinary work?
What can returning after distraction teach us about patience, and how does the purpose of the practice shape that return?
How could learning from yesterday’s consequences make today’s attention more useful to other people?

neighbors.invitation: Explore how concentrated reflection bears fruit in conduct.
Connect mindfulness with the daily review of what we have done.

references.label: 1 · Bhagavad Gita 6:26 — returning the wandering mind
references.note: Compare the recurring return of attention in this verse with remembrance in the heart and work of the hands. The Gita’s language of the Self deserves attention in its own setting; shared disciplines of concentration need not imply identical understandings of their object or goal.

subjects.introduction: My heart is constricted, we say in sorrow, and the heart stays exactly as it was. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá begins with that ordinary figure of speech to open a distinction He calls pivotal: some realities the senses meet, sun and sound and taste, while others, love, mind, grief, knowledge, have no place or outward form and can only be understood. Because nothing outside the senses is available for speech, every intelligible reality must be cast in a sensible mould to be spoken of at all, which is why mirrors, hearts and wombs do so much work in spiritual language and why reading them literally misleads. Plato’s divided line, with its visible images and intelligible objects, meets the same problem from another direction [1]. The distinction reaches far: to the spirit that neither enters nor leaves the body, to God’s knowing of things before they exist, to a world beyond death as unimaginable from here as this world is from the womb. The way continues into spirit and immateriality, into the seen and the hidden, and into the difference between sight and insight.
subjects.arc: Begin with a familiar metaphor, distinguish sensation from understanding, and explore what follows for spirit, divine knowledge, and the limits of description.

order.why: Examine the mind’s role and its own status as an intelligible reality.
shortened: Know that created things are of two kinds: material and spiritual, sensible and intelligible. That is, some are perceptible to the senses while others are only perceived by the mind.

Sensible realities are those which are perceived by the five outer senses: so, for example, those outward things which the eye sees are called sensible. Intelligible realities are those which have no outward existence but are perceived by the mind. For example, the mind itself is an intelligible reality and has no outward existence.

order.why: Begin with the familiar language of a heart constricted by sorrow.
shortened: But rational realities such as the intellect, the soul, love, sorrow, joy and the five inner faculties - if you wish to explain these you are compelled to cast them into sensible forms before explaining them.

For example, sorrow and grief, which are rational realities, you express through constriction, saying "My heart is constricted," whereas the heart remains in its original state, neither constricted nor expanded. But sorrow is a spiritual condition, and when you wish to express it you are compelled to make a comparison with sensible things.

order.why: Give that example a framework distinguishing sensible and intelligible realities.
shortened: The other kind of human knowledge is that of intelligible things; that is, it consists of intelligible realities which have no outward form or place and which are not sensible. For example, the power of the mind is not sensible, nor are any of the human attributes: These are intelligible realities. Love, likewise, is an intelligible and not a sensible reality. For the ear does not hear these realities, the eye does not see them, the smell does not sense them, the taste does not detect them, the touch does not perceive them.
But when you undertake to express these intelligible realities, you have no recourse but to cast them in the mould of the sensible, for outwardly there is nothing beyond the sensible.

order.why: Clearly distinguishes sensible and intelligible perceptions with examples of mathematical truths and spiritual attributes.
Pause over the distinction between seeing and the perceiving subject.
Consider changing sensible things alongside knowledge and understanding.
shortened: Sensible beings, for instance, include minerals, plants, and animals: those things which can be perceived with the physical senses; in other words, they can be seen with the eyes, heard with the ears, and smelled, touched, or tasted. All such things are subject to change. But those things perceptible to the intellect cannot be detected with these physical faculties. For example, knowledge and understanding are intelligible realities.

order.why: Explains intellect as a spiritual faculty that apprehends intelligible realities.
Return to metaphor as the means of communicating an abstract meaning.
shortened: Know thou that human perceptions are resolved into the intelligible and the sensible. The sensible, being that which is familiar and comprehensible, requireth no interpretation or allusion, but rather explanation and clarification. The intelligible, however, consisteth of spiritual realities that are intelligible rather than sensible--abstract, sanctified, and holy--having no outward forms whereby their expression might be readily achieved without metaphor and allusion.

order.why: Test spatial language against the relationship of spirit and body.
shortened: For otherwise, egress and regress, descent and inherence are characteristics of bodies and not of spirits--that is, egress and inherence pertain only to sensible realities, not to intelligible subtleties; and intelligible realities, such as reason, love, knowledge, imagination and thought, do not enter, exit or inhere, but rather denote relationships.

For example, knowledge, which is a form acquired by the mind, is an intelligible thing, and to speak of entering into the mind or exiting from it is absurd. Rather, it is a relationship of acquisition, even as images are reflected in a mirror.

order.why: Apply the distinction to the more demanding question of divine knowledge and concrete existence.
shortened: Existence is of two kinds: intelligible existence and concrete existence. Created things had intelligible existence before their concrete existence, meaning they were known to God, then they attained concrete existence, meaning they became realized externally. Sight has no connection to intelligible existence, it has connection to concrete existence.

The name "All-Seeing" is different from the name "All-Knowing." Created things were known to God, but the name "All-Seeing" had no connection to the realities of things. When they became realized in the world of existence, the name "All-Seeing" connected with them.

order.why: Let the womb comparison open reflection on a world beyond present experience.
shortened: The nature of the world to come is intelligible, not sensible, and its relationship and analogy is the analogy of this world in relation to the world of the womb. Is it possible to understand the faculties of hearing and sight, of cognition and apprehension in the womb, even in imagination? Nay, by God!

order.why: End the linked sequence with the difficulty of putting intellectual reality into words.
Revisit the human being as both a sensible creature and a knower.
shortened: The animals are keen in sensation, but man is endowed with piercing vision. Every moving creature apprehendeth sensible realities, but intelligible realities are disclosed and perceived by the seeing knower.

order.why: Ground the distinction again in love and sorrow.
Consider light as a model of intellectual disclosure.
Close with the flower’s attributes and the remaining question of its intrinsic essence.
shortened: When we consider the world of existence, we find that the essential reality underlying any given phenomenon is unknown. Phenomenal, or created, things are known to us only by their attributes. Man discerns only manifestations, or attributes, of objects, while the identity, or reality, of them remains hidden. For example, we call this object a flower. What do we understand by this name and title? We understand that the qualities appertaining to this organism are perceptible to us, but the intrinsic elemental reality, or identity, of it remains unknown.

questions: What do we mean when we say that love or sorrow is real, and how do we come to know it?
Where do the mirror, heart, and womb images help understanding, and where would reading them literally become misleading?
How does recognizing the mind as an object of inquiry change our confidence in its judgments?
What further questions arise when the distinction between sensible and intelligible is applied to divine knowledge or life beyond death?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the reliability and limits of the faculties through which we judge reality.
Consider why meanings require words even when words cannot contain them fully.

references.label: 1 · Plato, Republic VI, 509d–511e — the divided line
references.note: Near the end of Book VI, Plato distinguishes the visible and intelligible, then compares modes of inquiry within them. Read the use of a drawn geometrical figure beside the compilation’s use of sensible images for intelligible meanings. Where do the two accounts share a problem, and where do their explanations diverge?

subjects.introduction: Anyone who has tried to put love into a letter knows the double experience of needing words and finding them too small. Bahá’u’lláh and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá honour that experience without resolving it. Meaning, they teach, must take outward form in speech, and every language, Kurdish or Arabic, Persian or Pahlavi, is welcome so long as it carries meaning; yet words remain indications and allusions, signs pointing beyond themselves, while the realities of the spirit are inscribed on hearts rather than on paper. Words also change with time, so that what is plain today may need a gloss in a thousand years, and some truths wait for a season when they can be heard. The opening chapter of the Dao De Jing circles the same paradox, naming the Way while insisting that the enduring name cannot be spoken [1]. From here the path leads toward the Word of God and the limitations of those who receive it, toward the limits of the intellect, and finally toward the unknowability of God, where speech becomes, like a parent babbling to a child, an act of love.
subjects.arc: Start with a letter and an overflowing heart, explore the uses and limits of words, and end with speech adapted lovingly to a listener.

order.why: Open with the human warmth of correspondence and the heart’s living book.
shortened: O self-sacrificing servant of the Lord! Although writing and speaking can express what is in the heart, the realm of words falls short in fully conveying divine meanings. It is but an indication, an allusion, a sign. Therefore, the pages of hearts are open scrolls, and in them are inscribed the realities of spiritual feelings.
Despite these spiritual pages, it is strange that soul and heart still yearn for the tracings on paper, so that the essence of love may become evident and manifest in all degrees of existence.

order.why: Establish the necessity of outward form before examining its limits.
shortened: However, since the manifestation of meaning depends upon the world of words, and the emergence of spirits is conditioned and bound to the appearance of bodies - for every inner reality requires an outward form and every beginning demands an end - so that the form of the clot of blood, after ascending the heights of annihilation, might be honored with the robe of everlasting life - "Blessed be God, the best of creators" - and the essence of beginning, after returning from the realm of the divine identity, might appear in the garment of finality - "but he is the Apostle of God and the Seal of the Prophets" - so that the all-embracing word "He is the First and the Last, and the Manifest and the Hidden" might appear in the arena of existence.

order.why: Place meaning above the prestige of any particular language.
Connect diverse languages with the intentions they carry.
Introduce historical change in the meanings of expressions.
Extend that change toward the future reader’s need for explanation.
Examine the conflict that can follow attachment to names and words.
Consider metaphor as an indispensable way of conveying truth.
Bring together the limits of words, timing, and a hearer’s capacity. Revisit the garment of words and the responsibility of timing.
shortened: How many meanings are there that words cannot contain! How many of them have no expression and have been given neither statement nor allusion! And how many of them cannot be uttered because their time hath not come, as it hath been said: "Not all that is known can be disclosed, nor is the time ripe for all that can be disclosed, nor are the people capable of hearing all for which the time is ripe." And there are those whose mention dependeth upon knowledge of the Dawning-Places wherein We have expounded the sciences and revealed what was hidden.

order.why: Ask what contingent instruments can disclose about what transcends them.
shortened: Whoever contemplates the indications of that unique and eloquent sermon, speaking from the Tree of Praise, will testify that the description of the possible is itself possible, and the attribute of the dependent is dependent, and the kingdom endures in the kingdom. And concerning this matter, Al-Rida (peace be upon him) said: "Indeed, tools only define themselves, and instruments only point to their like, and in things their effects are found."

order.why: Press the distinction between allusion and reality.
Apply the problem of description to the soul’s world.
shortened: Understanding the world of souls is impossible in this world of bodies. That world is unlike anything you can conceive in your imagination. In these perishable bodies one cannot perceive the immortal worlds, save through that which ye sometimes behold in a dream.

order.why: Consider the intensity attributed to meanings beyond ordinary hearing.
shortened: Yet withal, I beseech Thee by the fire of Thy Being which hath ever been concealed in the mystery of Thine Essence, and by the ocean of Thy greatness which hath ever flowed in the reality of Thy Being, to teach me from Thy holy tongue which Thou hast sanctified from the hearing of Thy creation and hallowed from the understanding of Thy servants, and to honor me with the melodies of Thy rapture which none can hear, perceive, or know, for were but a single note thereof to appear, all who are in the heavens and on earth would be thunderstruck by the strange nature of its tune and the wondrous character of its pattern.

order.why: Distinguishes the divine Word from ordinary spoken and written words and their contingent limitations.
Let the riches of spirit test the resources of eloquence.
Return to love through the inexhaustible image of seas as ink.
shortened: In this hour when the hosts of holy fragrances and the waves of attraction are surging from all directions, and the might of the piercing meteor is driving away and casting out all people of vain imaginings, when the lights of the Kingdom are shining forth and the mysteries of the Realm of Power are manifesting and appearing, when the sea of favors is surging and the lamp of the gathering is brightly lit - this servant has made the pen a means to express the degrees of love for the Ancient Beauty, and has made words the interpreter of meanings, that perchance a verse from the scripture of attraction which is folded within the essence of the heart might be inscribed upon page and paper.
Alas! Alas! How could this be, even if all the seas were ink, and all the trees pens, and all the pages of the horizons were tablets.

order.why: End the linked sequence with words acknowledging their inability to encompass love.
shortened: This evanescent servant knoweth not what to say, having fallen into a world wherein he beholdeth the attributes of that Beloved One in such wise that no word is capable of describing them, nor qualified to define them. I swear by the Sun of utterance which hath shone forth from the most exalted station in all the world that no word can clothe the meaning of love for that Beloved One, nor can it reveal, indicate, describe or guide. Rather, in this station words remain silent, nay, prostrate, uttering only "I am the weakest of the weak."

order.why: Extend the question into prayer beyond syllables.
shortened: Adorn our bodies with the Robe of Thy Bounty and remove from our eyes the veil of sinfulness and give us the Chalice of Thy Grace, that the essence of all beings may sing Thy praise before the vision of Thy Grandeur. Reveal then Thyself, O Lord! by Thy merciful Utterance and the mystery of Thy Divine Being, that the holy ecstasy of prayer may fill our souls -- a prayer that shall rise above words and letters and transcend the murmur of syllables and sounds -- that all things may be merged into nothingness before the revelation of Thy Splendour.

order.why: Let the supplied Zhuangzi passage distinguish the instrument from the meaning sought.
Place a Christian mystical voice beside the problem of describing God.
Retain the severe counsel about entrusted knowledge and the judgment its communication requires.
shortened: It behooveth the wayfarer to guard this knowledge deposited in the receptacles of enlightened hearts by God the creator of mankind, to protect it as his eyes, and to conceal it in his breast. Were he to reveal one letter of these secrets other than to those who are worthy, he shall have perpetuated three serious crimes. The first is betrayal inasmuch as he hath betrayed God by exposing His mysteries to those unsuited to hear them. The second is injustice inasmuch as he conferred this station upon one who doth not deserve it, and weighed him down with an unbearable load he cannot carry.

The third is murder because he misled this wretched one and killed him by killing his faith, inasmuch as he was unable to comprehend this divine knowledge, his feet slipped from whence he had progressed in the Cause of his Origin and Return.

order.why: Close with Rumi’s image of a teacher’s compassionate adaptation to a learner.
shortened: For a newborn child the father makes babbling sounds, though his intellect may make a survey of the (whole) world.... For the sake of teaching that tongue-tied (child), one must go outside of one's own language (customary manner of speech). You must come into (adopt) his language, in order that he may learn knowledge and science from you. All the people, then, are as his [the spiritual masters] children: this (fact) is necessary for the Pir [the master] (to bear in mind) when he gives (them) instruction.

questions: How can words be indispensable to understanding while also becoming an obstacle to it?
What helps us recognize whether a disagreement concerns words, meanings, or the realities those meanings point toward?
How might changing language and the listener’s capacity affect the way we read a sacred passage or share an insight?
What can the compilation’s varied images of love, silence, and teaching suggest about speaking faithfully when complete expression is impossible?

neighbors.invitation: Investigate why intelligible meanings are communicated through sensible images.
Consider the discernment involved in remaining silent or beginning to speak.

references.label: 1 · Dao De Jing, chapter 1 — the name and the enduring Way
references.note: In James Legge’s translation, the opening chapter distinguishes a name that can be spoken from the enduring name. Compare that problem with the compilation’s insistence that meaning needs expression yet exceeds it. How does each text use language to awaken attention to language’s limits?

subjects.introduction: Strength that exceeds its bounds turns into weakness, Bahá’u’lláh warns, and in that reversal moderation stops being a timid virtue and becomes an art of judgment. Everything has its station, measure and limit; life in the contingent world depends on measure and timely action together, so that the right thing done at the wrong moment can still destroy. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá will not deprecate comfort, admitting He would move to a better house if He found one, but He refuses a life developed on one side only, whether the ideal or the physical, and He extends the same proportion to wealth, to the speed of ships and trains, and to the pace of a whole civilization. The body itself teaches the lesson: health is an equilibrium of elements, and illness the surfeit of one against another. The Buddha asking Soṇa how a lute sounds when its strings are too tight or too slack makes the same point about effort [1], and what a practitioner must learn to notice. The way continues toward health and healing, toward frugality and simplicity, and toward the moderation of wealth and poverty.
subjects.arc: Begin with strength becoming weakness, apply proportion to personal and social life, and conclude with gradual growth and the harmony that sustains existence.

order.why: Open with the striking reversal of strength into weakness.
shortened: Moderation is necessary in all things, for if strength exceedeth its bounds it turneth into weakness.

O friends! The Most Exalted Pen counseleth you and biddeth you to that which exalteth the Word of God and uplifteth souls. Hold fast unto moderation in all conditions and speak with equity in all matters.

order.why: Give the reversal its language of station, measure, and limit.
shortened: For all things there is fixed a station, measure and limit.

order.why: Add timing to the question of appropriate measure.
Bring spiritual and physical development into the same life.
Explore moderation as a condition for growing spiritual capacity.
Consider balance through changes of fortune.
shortened: When fate approaches, be not elated, and when it retreats be not saddened, and when it smiles do not laugh, and when it frowns and darkens do not be disturbed or anxious. You must practice moderation, you must rely on God, you must be balanced.

order.why: Introduce the daily rhythm of work and rest as described in the source.
Apply measure to conduct in a particular social setting.
Consider the consequences of public display and the need for wisdom.
shortened: However, do not set aside wisdom. Grand displays and demonstrations cause envy and tumult among the deniers. It is better to observe moderation.

order.why: Bring proportion into the organization of economic life.
Extend moderation to the scale and speed of technological undertakings.
Explains why even beneficial things become harmful when carried beyond moderation.
Connect peace and coordination with the composition of living things.
Introduce the source’s bodily account of proportionate elements.
Keep the overlapping selections together in their fuller explanation of bodily equilibrium.
shortened: As to physical agents, which are the primary cause of illness, their effect is due to the following: The human body is composed of numerous elements according to a particular state of equilibrium. So long as this equilibrium is maintained, man is preserved from sickness, but should this fundamental balance, which is the central requirement of a sound constitution, be upset, the constitution will be disrupted and illnesses will supervene.
For instance, if there is a deficiency in one of the component parts of the body and a surfeit of another, the state of equilibrium is disturbed and illness occurs.

order.why: Complete the linked group of historical explanations concerning food and balance.
Open a different application of the language of extremes: divine bestowal and human action.
Turn the search for balance into a prayer.
Preserve the supplied account of elemental balance in its own cosmological terms.
Let a tree’s gradual fruitfulness suggest a rhythm for action.
End with harmony and intermingling as images of renewed life.
Let the warning about civilization enlarge that danger to a social scale.

questions: What signs might tell us that a strength, comfort, or worthwhile ambition is beginning to undermine another good?
How do measure and timing work together, and when might moderation require decisive action?
What does the image of tuning an instrument add to the compilation’s images of bodily balance and gradual growth?
How could a community judge the scale and pace of material progress in relation to spiritual development and the well-being of its members?

neighbors.invitation: Explore how a rhythm of rest makes room for renewal and reflection.
Read measured judgment alongside steadfastness under pressure.

references.label: 1 · Aṅguttara Nikāya 6.55, Soṇa Sutta — tuning effort
references.note: The Buddha asks Soṇa to recall how strings sound when too tight, too loose, or properly tuned, then applies the analogy to persistence. Compare this responsive adjustment of effort with the compilation’s relationship between strength, limits, and timely action. What must a practitioner learn to notice?

subjects.introduction: Spread wide the feast of fellowship, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá urges, and show hospitality even to wild beasts and birds. The welcome is not sentimental. Animals share with us the selfsame physical feelings, he explains, and because they cannot speak their pain, we owe them a consideration even greater than we owe our fellow man. So compassion receives tasks: feed the hungry creature, let the weary one rest, teach children to heal a sick animal, train a horse without striking it, as the Arabs do. A beaten dog is ordered two loaves of bread and meat every day; a dog shown one kindness never forgets. Harder questions follow about hunting, about the lamb killed for the table, about the limits of human power over vulnerable life, and they deserve to be read with care for each source’s setting. The Qur’án’s description of the creatures of the earth and the birds as communities like our own widens the circle further [1]. The road from here runs into compassion and kindness as such, into the assistance of the poor, the orphan and the sick, and into the questions of diet and of the animal kingdom itself.
subjects.arc: Extend hospitality beyond the human guest, practice tenderness in ordinary care, and examine the responsibilities that accompany power over animal life.

order.why: Translate that welcome into specific habits children can learn. Revisit shared feeling and the special vulnerability of animals.
Open by extending the familiar practice of hospitality to animals.
shortened: Seek security and peace, and spread wide the feast of fellowship. Even show hospitality to wild beasts and birds, and show kindness to enemies and ill-wishers.

order.why: Let the care of birds and their young make nurture tangible.
Introduce a concrete act of provision for an injured dog.
Contrast striking an animal with training it well.
Use the satirical seminary anecdote to expose thoughtless cruelty.
Attend to the enduring response a single kindness can evoke.
Develop the shared feelings that ground mercy, extending the concern to plants.
Pause over the explicit importance accorded to kindness to animals.
Distinguishes permission to eat meat from the compassion that recoils from slaughtering animals.
Bring pain and the human use of animals for food into the inquiry.
Retain the reported response to the killing of birds and animals.
Place a particular warning against killing birds beside those reflections.
shortened: The Blessed Beauty knowing his love for hunting told him: 'Don't kill these innocent birds.' But the man paid no attention. Without exaggeration he fired on that day five or six hundred shots but without killing one bird.

order.why: Read the legal permission concerning hunting together with its restraint against excess.
Explore protection, gentleness, and restraint in relation to hunting.
shortened: In many countries of the West, laws are enacted to restrict the cruelty of man toward animals and in some states they are hunted only at certain seasons. When I was in America I went through several large zoological gardens, some of which covered many acres. In these gardens hunting is strictly prohibited. There are other large national Parks in Western America which I have not seen, where I have been told, gazelle and deer roam at will and man is not allowed to interfere with their freedom. In these places the animals become so tame that they associate with man. how ideal this is, how perfect, how good!

order.why: End the linked readings by carrying affection for a faithful animal back into human relationships.
Give that vulnerability the practical answer of comfort and protection.
shortened: O thou my dear heavenly daughter!
To the people of truth, animal, like unto man, is very dear. Therefore, man should be kind to both man and animal, and should strive as much as possible towards the comfort and protection of animals.

order.why: Let the faithful dog’s story deepen attention to companionship.
shortened: The Arab replied: 'This animal has always been my companion; whether at home or on the road he has faithfully guarded me against danger, and now he is dying of starvation in this barren wilderness and I am left utterly powerless to save his life.'

The Arab's lament grew louder: 'But this is not an animal, this is a trained dog who has been my constant companion, accompanying me on all my travels. It has performed good and faithful service and has rescued me many a time from life-threatening danger.'

order.why: Retain the supplied reflection on suffering in living organisms.
Keep the difficult historical discussion of diet and experimentation within the ethical inquiry.
Introduce the distinction drawn between instinctive affection and moral choice.
shortened: The love shown by animals is instinctive and not dependent upon their own will--that is, they are endowed with their qualities and use them in a natural way, but not by their own will. As these qualities are instinctive and not voluntary, animals will not be rewarded. Their benefits are confined to this word only.

order.why: Close by asking how care for animals enlarges the responsibility of human speech.
shortened: He should consume every wayward thought with the flame of His loving mention, and, with the swiftness of lightning, pass by all else save Him. He should succor the dispossessed, and never withhold his favor from the destitute. He should show kindness to animals, how much more unto his fellowman, to him who is endowed with the power of utterance.

questions: What might hospitality mean when the being who needs it cannot explain its hunger, pain, or fear to us?
How do the passages about children and training suggest ways of learning compassion through practice?
How can we read the passages on hunting, food, and restraint together while attending carefully to their different settings and kinds of authority?
What does the compilation’s movement between human and animal relationships reveal about the reach of mercy?

neighbors.invitation: Follow mercy across human, animal, and plant life.
Consider a generosity whose reach does not depend on repayment.

references.label: 1 · Qur’an 6:38 — communities of living creatures
references.note: The verse places creatures of earth and birds within communities and a relationship to their Lord. Compare that widening of attention with the compilation’s appeal to shared feeling. What responsibilities might each way of seeing make easier to recognize? The page offers several English translations.

subjects.introduction: Nature, Bahá’u’lláh says, is in its essence the embodiment of His name the Creator, the expression of God’s Will in and through the contingent world, and a person of insight sees nothing in it but that splendour. The claim invites contemplation and immediately raises a difficulty. Fire burns and water flows without any awareness of doing so; nature has neither consciousness nor will, and yet it is full of order and law, which is ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s reason for placing it in the grasp of a Lord who rules it. Human beings are the exception, able to discover the natures of things and so to master them, and every craft comes from that discovery. Psalm 19 sings of heavens that declare the glory of God and a sun that runs its daily course [1], another way of reading creation as speech. But is seeing God in nature enough? ‘Abdu’l-Bahá tells of a traveller dying of thirst who spies an oasis and knows there must be water; conviction does not quench thirst, and he must find the spring, which is why belief in nature’s God has never founded a civilisation while revelation has. The subject opens onto the Primal Will, the imperfection of nature, the power of the mind over it, and the single law that runs through all things.
subjects.arc: Encounter nature as a sign of divine creativity, examine natural order and human choice, and carry contemplation of creation toward revelation and conduct.

order.why: Open with the central passage on nature as the expression of the Creator’s name and will.
shortened: Say: Nature in its essence is the embodiment of My Name, the Maker, the Creator. Its manifestations are diversified by varying causes, and in this diversity there are signs for men of discernment. Nature is God's Will and is its expression in and through the contingent world. It is a dispensation of Providence ordained by the Ordainer, the All-Wise.

order.why: Examine the philosophical use of nature as a source of observable phenomena. Bring the Creative Name and the Primal Will back into relationship.
shortened: They attribute all these conditions and phenomena, even the movement of the chain of beings and their development and growth, to Nature, and consider Nature as the source of all beings. He says that the Nature which they consider as the source of all beings is the manifestation of His Creative Name. That is to say, the Holy Essence is sanctified from all names and attributes, even from being known as the First Cause. It is the First Cause that is the source of all being and which has been interpreted as Nature.

order.why: Explains human powers above nature as means of giving material expression to the will of God.
Consider nature itself as an intelligible rather than directly sensible reality.
Ground the question of volition in familiar natural processes and human discovery. Keep the distinct, fuller supplied wording of that argument.
shortened: When you consider nature itself, however, you see that it has neither awareness nor will. For instance, the nature of fire is to burn; it burns without consciousness or will. The nature of water is to flow; it flows without consciousness or will.
It is therefore evident that the natural movements of all created things are compelled, and that nothing moves of its own will save animals and, in particular, man.
Man is able to resist and oppose nature inasmuch as he discovers the natures of things and, by virtue of this discovery, has mastery over nature itself.

order.why: Condense the contrast between natural compulsion and human will.
Retain the reported account of the Primal Will unfolding through levels of life.
shortened: The atoms of the elements are predisposed (programmed) to synthesis and composition according to the laws of nature; the Cosmic Spirit, the divine Primal Will operates and creates in this manner. The Primal Will operates in the element, in the primal atom, as attraction and repulsion; on the next higher level as organic life; then as animal-vegetative; and finally as spiritual life, which is destined to rise to the super-spiritual.

order.why: Explore the language of a power sustaining phenomena through its bounty.
Introduce the warning against separating nature from its Creator.
Let the thirsty traveler’s story give the question of revelation a human urgency.
shortened: When Khan was in the Holy Land, 'Abdu'l-Baha made this reply to an American inquirer: There was once an Arab traveler who had lost his way in the desert. He was dying of thirst and, humbly, he begged God for water. Suddenly on the far horizon he saw an oasis with waving trees, and he knew that there could be no trees and greenery unless water was present too. When he had somehow dragged himself across the sands and reached the oasis, how did he go about quenching his thirst? Was his conviction enough for him, that growing things meant water? Or did he search avidly for a source, a crack in a rock or an opening in the earth where water could get through and he could drink and live?

Believing that God is present in nature has never been enough. This belief has never founded, and could never found, a civilization. But belief in God's Chosen Ones, His Prophets, through Whom come the living waters of His revelation, has created structures in the life of man that the revolution of many ages and cycles could not destroy, and brought him holy light that time could never dim.

order.why: Turn from natural law toward the relationship of divine law, reason, and justice.
shortened: 'The Laws of God are not imposition of will, or of power, or pleasure, but the resolutions of truth, reason and justice.'

order.why: Revisit the distinction between inherent properties and volition.
Compare natural laws with ideals realized through the Manifestations.
Preserve the supplied distinction between nature as creature and an eternal divine order.
shortened: Nature did not originate of itself - by accident, - but it sprang from a divine act of creation. Thus nature does not represent an eternal, divine order, but it is a creature, a work of temporal existence, for what can be created, the Creator can also make to vanish.

order.why: Retain the imported reading pointer in its supplied form.
Introduce the question of miracle and the limits of human reason.
Open the supplied philosophical conversation about divine breath and form.
Follow the fuller treatment of nature and the breath of the Merciful.

questions: How does distinguishing an expression of divine will from conscious choice help us read the passages about nature together?
What do the images of the heavens and the thirsty traveler suggest about the relationship between recognizing a sign and responding to it?
How might human discovery and the ability to alter natural processes enlarge our responsibilities within creation?
Which uses of the word nature in these readings need to be distinguished before we compare their philosophical or religious claims?
How could contemplating creation influence the conduct through which we seek to express justice and goodness?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the distinction between a sensible phenomenon and an intelligible reality.
Explore how the pursuit of knowledge and religious purpose can inform one another.

references.label: 1 · Psalm 19:1–6 — creation declaring divine glory
references.note: Read the psalm’s sky, recurring days, and journeying sun beside nature as an expression of the Creator’s name. Both invite contemplation through images of the natural world. What is conveyed by their imagery, and what further questions about revelation remain open?

subjects.introduction: When a life is purely moral, ‘Abdu’l-Bahá says, the insincere learn sincerity from it, the faithless become faithful, and the cowardly find courage, simply by coming into contact with it. Example works without argument. Bahá’u’lláh asks that our acts be a guide to all humankind, and the Báb points to His own years as a merchant as a pattern for every transaction. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá, whose own conduct the friends were told to follow, knew that all eyes were fixed on those who lived beneath the Shrine, and He resisted every difficulty so that others might learn to do the same. The power is double-edged: the wish to be admired can hollow out the very conduct that inspires, which is why enduring influence rests on private character, on fellowship, and on deeds that make spoken conviction credible. Confucius’ ruler who governs by virtue and so becomes a pole star around which the others turn offers an older picture of character’s quiet pull [1]. The way leads on to goodly deeds, to the virtuous life as it is walked day by day, and to the conduct that marks a true believer.
subjects.arc: Begin with character’s effect on others, explore example in work and relationships, and test public influence against private sincerity.

order.why: Open with the transformation made imaginable by contact with a moral life.
Consider acts as a guide through which teachings become recognizable.
Give example an ordinary practical setting in commercial dealings.
Introduce the explicit invitation to follow ‘Abdu’l-Bahá’s conduct.
Explore example under difficulty and the purpose that sustains it.
Bring imitation and gratitude into a particular family relationship.
shortened: Praise be to God, you too have followed his example, becoming a manifestation of "the son is the secret of his father."

To the extent possible, walk in his path and follow his example in all things, so that you may spend your days in the best of gifts, discover the treasure of the Kingdom, and become a manifestation of "God will enrich all from His abundance."

order.why: Consider the responsibility of already being an example to others.
shortened: Wherefore, give thanks unto God inasmuch as He hath made you exemplars unto His loved ones. And in you is an excellent example for them to follow in the path of God.

order.why: Make that responsibility vivid through visitors whose spirits may be renewed.
Widen the hoped-for influence of good character.
shortened: And now, I hope that thou shalt become the cause of the illumination of souls, so that they may acquire a heavenly nature, and that thy goodly character may exert its influence upon a vast number of people.

order.why: Explains in detail why demonstrating virtues has more educational effect than merely recommending them.
Let the image of light join personal conduct with a wider human horizon.
shortened: Any of the friends who conduct themselves according to the divine teachings become a light to the human world and a brilliant star in the horizon of eternal glory.

order.why: End the linked sequence with deeds that can illuminate recognition across peoples.
shortened: Holy and assured souls must manifest such deeds and character as are befitting, that all the peoples of the earth may follow their example, so that the light of recognition may encompass and illumine the world.

order.why: Ask what makes an example endure in historical memory.
Locate the basis of lasting influence in inner life and private character.
Open the practice of example to different capacities through everyday help and hospitality.
Close with loving fellowship and kindness that make faith visible in deed.

questions: What have you learned from another person’s conduct that their words alone could not have taught you?
How might we follow an example thoughtfully while responding to the different circumstances and capacities of our own lives?
What helps public conduct remain connected to private character when we know that others are watching?
How could kindness in an ordinary transaction or difficult relationship make a spiritual principle more understandable to someone else?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the desire for recognition alongside the wish to serve.
Consider the concrete acts through which a compassionate example becomes visible.

references.label: 1 · Confucius, Analects 2.1 and 2.3 — leading through virtue
references.note: At the opening of Book II, the image of a steady pole star introduces government through virtue; the next comparison concerns punishment, propriety, and inward moral response. How does this political setting illuminate—and differ from—the compilation’s account of example in the life of every believer? James Legge’s translation is provided.

subjects.introduction: Of all pilgrimages, runs an old saying the friends were reminded of, the greatest is to relieve a sorrow-laden heart. Compassion in the Bahá’í writings starts there, in the practical relief of one person’s grief, and ‘Abdu’l-Bahá makes it the measure of human goodness: the best person is the one who gladdens the broken-hearted, the worst the one who causes a heart pain. If prayer itself cannot free you from anger or depression, He advises, go at once and give pleasure to someone sorrowful. The forms are concrete and ordinary: shelter for the stranger, companionship for the lonely, water for the thirsty, a father’s tenderness toward relatives, enemies, animals and even plants. Kindness is to be a ray of God shining on this one and that one without choosing, yet it keeps company with truthfulness and wisdom, and there are moments when an apparent kindness only lets harm continue. The Samaritan who bandaged the wounded traveller and then paid for his continued care shows the same love carried through to its practical end [1]. The path leads on through loving all and consorting with all, through generosity, and through the kindness owed to animals.
subjects.arc: Begin with the relief of a sorrowing heart, widen compassion through concrete relationships, and examine the wisdom required for care that truly helps.

order.why: Widen compassion through concrete roles toward the orphan, the old, the thirsty, and the poor.
shortened: O ye lovers of God! Be kind to all peoples; care for every person; do all ye can to purify the hearts and minds of men; strive ye to gladden every soul. To every meadow be a shower of grace, to every tree the water of life; be as sweet musk to the sense of humankind, and to the ailing be a fresh, restoring breeze. Be pleasing waters to all those who thirst, a careful guide to all who have lost their way; be father and mother to the orphan, be loving sons and daughters to the old, be an abundant treasure to the poor.

order.why: Open with the arresting description of relieving sorrow as the greatest pilgrimage.
shortened: Remember the saying: 'Of all pilgrimages the greatest is to relieve the sorrow-laden heart.'

order.why: Place the gladdening of a broken heart at the center of human goodness.
Turn that vision into an immediate call to help someone who suffers.
shortened: But if you are so angry, so depressed and so sore that your spirit cannot find deliverance and peace even in prayer, then quickly go and give some pleasure to someone lowly or sorrowful, or to a guilty or innocent sufferer!

order.why: Attend to the stranger, the solitary person, and the wounded.
shortened: Therefore, as much as you can, bring joy to hearts and glad tidings to souls. Be a refuge and shelter for strangers, and grant those who are alone assistance and support. Be a remedy for every pain and a balm for every wound.

order.why: Make companionship a source of hope for grief.
Sustain the healing image in care for the helpless. Preserve the separate supplied wording of the healing image.
shortened: O respected companion! Remain firm in the Covenant and be steadfast and unwavering. Remember the friends and be a companion to the loved ones. Console the helpless and be kind to the distressed. Be a healing balm to every wound and the greatest remedy for every ailment.

order.why: Connect material needs with the restoration of dignity. Widen companionship across peoples through sympathy and courtesy.
shortened: O thou maid-servant of God! The utmost desire of the lordly ones is the union of the friends, the agreement of the believers and the spiritual communication of the hearts; in order that they may shine in this darkened world like unto bright stars; educate all the communities of the world in the precepts of love; be kind and benevolent to every one, sympathetic and compassionate to all; to become the cool and pure water to every thirsty one, a heavenly table to every hungry one, a swift healing antidote to every sick one and the cause of the everlasting glory to every humiliated one.

order.why: Let the parental image widen responsibility toward humanity.
Gives concrete instructions to answer avoidance, harm and insults with continued kindness and fellowship.
Return to the intimate setting of relatives.
Notice the joy one friend can bring another.
shortened: Whenever a friend gladdens the heart of a friend and shows kindness, this heart finds the utmost joy and delight.

order.why: Give tenderness an ordinary form in association and invitation.
Extend companionship from friend to stranger in gratitude to God.
Challenge the reader to consider kindness even toward enemies.
Reaffirm well-wishing toward all.
shortened: The friends and handmaidens of the Merciful must be well-wishers and kind to all.

order.why: Ask what spiritual motive can sustain love beyond repayment.
shortened: You must be exceedingly compassionate to each other and to all the people of the world. Love and serve mankind just for the sake of God and not for anything else. The foundation of your love toward humanity must be spiritual faith and divine assurance.

order.why: Read kindness alongside the patience that lets it endure.
shortened: After the grace of God and divine favors, thou hast not transgressed, nor dost thou transgress, the binding and decisive commandments that have been revealed and sent down in the Tablets from the Supreme Pen, and thou hast been and art dealing with all souls with utmost kindness, love and patience, according to His command.

order.why: Consider kindness as a capacity to increase day by day.
shortened: He is now extremely satisfied that you have engaged him in work, and surely day by day increase your love and kindness, for this is the cause of attaining God's good pleasure and my happiness.

order.why: Let the seed image suggest the patience of cultivation.
Place that cultivation within the language of divine mercy.
shortened: As much as thou canst, be thou a manifestation of the favors of the Merciful and an angel of the mercy of God.

order.why: Name kindness as a fundamental principle of the teachings.
Pause over the urgency of avoiding injury to hope and the heart.
shortened: Beware!  Beware!  Lest ye offend any heart.
Beware!  Beware!  Lest ye hurt any soul.
Beware!  Beware!  Lest ye deal unkindly toward any person.
Beware!  Beware!  Lest ye be the cause of hopelessness to any creature.

order.why: Consider the inward effect of one’s conduct on others.
Bring care for feeling into the delivery of difficult news.
shortened: When I have bad news for someone, I do not convey it to him openly, rather do I converse with him in such wise that when he heareth that news, my words bring comfort to him.

order.why: Read kindness together with truthfulness and reciprocal service.
shortened: Fourth--They must observe the utmost kindness, so that all may consider themselves servants of each other, and be truthful and honest to all mankind.

order.why: Introduce the explicit relationship of kindness and wisdom.
shortened: The friends of God must show complete wisdom and kindness to all, displaying good conduct, so it becomes clear and evident that these souls are the essence of bounty, the reality of mercy, the essence of favors, and pure justice and fairness.

order.why: Sustain the pairing of compassion and considered judgment.
shortened: We counsel thee to observe wisdom, for the people are weak. The Lord, exalted be His glory, hath shown forbearance out of pure grace. Therefore must all be mindful of wisdom and treat mankind with kindliness and compassion.

order.why: Retain both the fundamental principle and its demanding exception, inviting the full context on enabling harm.
Read another specific qualification alongside the wide invitation to comfort and shelter.
Extend mercy to the feelings of animals and the nurture of plants.
Make the response to kindness tangible through a dog’s memory.
Consider the relationship of service, kindness, and spiritual guidance.
Close the linked sequence with happiness joined to the welfare of others.
Resume with the supplied brief call to kindness.
shortened: Kindness is a ray of God, and graciousness the brightness of heaven; yet in pure hearts there is light, while in sorrow-laden souls there is darkness. Look not upon this one or that one: be thou kind.

order.why: Attend again to those who have fallen or lost hope.
Let service to humanity become a task shared by every member.
shortened: Each member must try to be kind to everyone and to show forth great affection towards every living soul.

order.why: Bring the material and spiritual needs of others together in practical care.
shortened: Be always kind to everyone and a refuge for those who are without shelter.
Be daughters to those who are older than you.
Be sisters to those who are of your own age.
Be mothers to those who are younger than yourselves.

questions: How does the opening image of pilgrimage change what we understand as a spiritual achievement?
Which kinds of suffering are easiest for us to notice, and which forms of companionship or care might we overlook?
How can kindness, truthfulness, and wisdom work together when comforting someone, conveying difficult news, or responding to harmful behavior?
What changes when compassion extends beyond friends and familiar people to enemies, animals, and other living things?
How might the Good Samaritan’s sustained practical care help us translate one of this compilation’s images into a lasting habit?

neighbors.invitation: Examine the inward injuries that words and conduct can cause or help to heal.
Follow compassion into the sharing of resources, comfort, and knowledge.

references.label: 1 · Luke 10:25–37 — the Good Samaritan
references.note: Follow the Samaritan’s attention from seeing the wounded traveler to providing immediate care and arranging continuing support. Compare this sequence of acts with the compilation’s images of balm, refuge, and companionship. How is the meaning of neighbor disclosed through what someone does?
